Why? Because it is impossible for a cause and the phenomenon that possesses the cause to arise either at a prior time, a subsequent time, or simultaneously.
As it is said: "If phenomena— whether prior, posterior, or simultaneous— are all unestablished,
then since these phenomena arise from causes, how could they ever be established?"
To claim that the cause exists first and the effect exists later is not tenable. Why?
If the effect were produced from a cause that existed later, then at the time when the cause was prior, the cause would not yet exist; of what, then, would it be the cause?
If the cause existed prior to that which possesses the cause, then that which possesses the cause would already be established even in the absence of a cause; what need would there be for a cause?

If the cause and that which possesses the cause exist simultaneously, this too is without causality, just as when the two horns of an ox grow at the same time, they do not serve as causes for one another.
In this way, the cause is not the cause of the effect, and the effect is not the effect of the cause, because they arise simultaneously.
Therefore, the causal relationship across the three times cannot be established.
Question: "Your refutation of the law of cause and effect is not established even within the three times.
If the refutation existed first and the object to be refuted existed later, then since the object to be refuted does not yet exist, what would that refutation refute?"
If that which is to be refuted exists first and the refutation exists later, then since that which is to be refuted is already established, what is the use of a refutation?

If the refutation and that which is to be refuted exist simultaneously, this too would lack a causal relationship, just as when the two horns of a cow grow simultaneously, the left and right do not depend upon one another.
"In this way, the refutation does not depend on the refutable, and the refutable does not depend on the refutation. He replied:
"Within your refutation of the refutable, there is likewise this same fault."
If all phenomena are empty, then there is neither that which refutes nor that which is refuted; thus, my current exposition of emptiness establishes what I have asserted.
If I were to assert that the refuter and the refuted definitely exist, then this objection would be valid;
however, since I do not assert that the refuter and the refuted definitely exist, this objection should not be raised.
Question: "The eye perceives causes from the past, such as a potter making a jar.
It also perceives causes from the future, such as having a disciple because of oneself; once one has instructed a disciple, one subsequently recognizes them as a disciple."
There is also the cause of simultaneity, as in the case of a lamp and its light.
If one were to say that a prior-time cause, a posterior-time cause, and a simultaneous cause are unattainable, this would not be correct.
He replied: "The analogy of a potter making a jar is not appropriate. Why is this so?"
If the jar does not yet exist, with whom would the potter act as a cause?
As with the potter, all prior causes are likewise unobtainable;
posterior causes are similarly unobtainable. If the disciple does not yet exist, who would be this teacher?
Therefore, even at a later time, a cause cannot be established.

If one asserts that cause and effect exist simultaneously, like a lamp and its light, this too is equivalent to a doubtful cause; since the lamp and the light arise at the same time, how can they be mutually dependent?
Because such causes and conditions are empty, one should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and sentient beings are all empty.
12. Contemplation of the Gate of Arising (*Utpāda-mukha-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, all phenomena are empty.

Why is this? Because arising, non-arising, and the time of arising cannot be apprehended; thus, that which has already arisen does not arise, that which has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which is in the process of arising does not arise either.
As it is said:
That which has already arisen does not arise; that which has not yet arisen also does not arise.
Apart from what has arisen and what has not arisen, there is no arising at the very moment of arising.

"Arising" (*jāti*) is named as the emergence and appearance of a fruit; "unarisen" is named as that which has not yet emerged, has not yet appeared, and does not yet exist; "the time of arising" is named as the initial emergence that is not yet complete.
Regarding the statement "that which arises does not give rise to the fruit": this means that once arising has already arisen, it does not arise again.
Why is this? Because it would entail the fallacy of infinite regress, as that which has already been produced would be produced again.

If a birth, having already arisen, were to produce a second birth; and that second birth, having already arisen, were to produce a third birth; and that third birth, having already arisen, were to produce a fourth birth; [then this fault would follow].
If there were a second birth for that which has already been born as its first birth, then such births would be infinite.
This is not the case; therefore, birth is non-birth.
Furthermore, if one claims that the "birth of birth" and the "birth of what has already been born" are both instances where birth arises through non-birth.

This is not so. Why? Because if that which has already arisen were to arise again, there would be two kinds of arising: [the arising of what has already arisen and the arising of what was previously unarisen].
Since that which has already arisen arises, and that which has not yet arisen arises, your previous definitive statement is now rendered indefinite.

Just as what has been done should not be done again, what has been burned should not be burned again, and what has been realized should not be realized again, so too, what has already arisen should not arise again;
therefore, the dharma of arising does not arise.
The non-arising dharma also does not arise. Why? Because it is not conjoined with arising;
furthermore, because [otherwise] there would be the fault of attributing arising to all that is non-arising.
If a non-arising dharma were to arise, then there would be arising apart from the act of arising, which is itself non-arising.

If there were arising apart from the act of arising, then there would be acting apart from the act of acting, going apart from the act of going, and eating apart from the act of eating; such a view would destroy conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-dharma*).
This is not so; therefore, a non-arising dharma does not arise.
Furthermore, if a non-arising dharma were to arise, then all non-arising dharmas would necessarily arise:

all ordinary beings who have not yet produced *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* would necessarily produce it; the afflictions of an Arhat of the indestructible nature (*avinipāta-dharman*), which do not arise, would arise; and the horns of rabbits, horses, and the like, which do not arise, would arise.
This is not so; therefore, one should not say that what is unarisen arises. Question:

"Regarding 'the unarisen arising,' it is like when causes and conditions assemble at a specific time and place, and through the perfection of skillful means, that which was unarisen then arises. It is not the case that everything arises from being unarisen; therefore, one should not raise the objection that everything arises from being unarisen."

He replied: "If a phenomenon arises only when there is an agent, produced through the conjunction of skillful means and various conditions, then within this process, that which already exists does not arise; that which does not yet exist does not arise; and that which both exists and does not exist also does not arise. Thus, as previously stated, these three ways of seeking its arising cannot be found."
Therefore, a dharma that has not yet arisen does not arise.
Nor does it arise at the time of arising. Why is this?
There is the fault of "the arising of arising," because it would entail the fault of that which has not yet arisen coming into being.
Regarding a phenomenon at the time of its arising: the portion already arisen does not arise, as previously explained;
the portion not yet arisen also does not arise, as previously explained.

Furthermore, if there were a time of arising apart from the process of arising, then it would follow that arising occurs at that time; however, in reality, there is no time of arising apart from the process of arising. Therefore, even the "time of arising" does not arise.
Furthermore, if one were to say that "at the time of arising, there is arising," then there would be two arisings:
first, taking the time of arising as the arising itself; second, arising at the time of arising.
There are no two dharmas; how can one speak of two types of arising?
Therefore, at the time of arising, there is also no arising.
Furthermore, when arising has not yet occurred, there is no "time of arising"; where, then, could arising proceed?
If arising has no place of occurrence, then there is no arising at the time of arising; therefore, even at the time of arising, there is no arising.
Thus, arising, non-arising, and the time of arising are all unestablished, because the phenomenon of arising is unestablished.
Non-arising is likewise for abiding and ceasing.
Because arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are also not established;
because conditioned phenomena are not established, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are also not established.
Because conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are not established, sentient beings are also not established.
Therefore, one should know that all phenomena are unborn, for they are ultimately empty and quiescent.
